newsitem.title: USA: Florida tourist chiefs dispute sheriff over safety.
newsitem.headline: Florida tourist chiefs dispute sheriff over safety.

text.p: Florida tourist officials scrambled to salvage the state's tarnished image as a vacation paradise on Monday after a county sheriff went on national television and warned visitors to stay away from the state.

They blasted Sheriff John McDougall of Lee County in southwestern Florida, criticizing his remarks and faulting his logic while emphasizing how crime in Florida had dropped through aggressive policing.

McDougall rattled the tourist industry when he said on NBC's Today show on Friday the state was too dangerous for tourists because of a U.S. Supreme Court ruling freeing hundreds of violent felons from prison.
"I wouldn't tell anyone, wouldn't even tell my family, to come," the outspoken McDougall, who has been sheriff for eight years, said. "I think it's very dangerous."

His comments made news not only in the United States but in Europe, where fear of crime cut the number of tourists visiting the state. Nine European tourists were murdered in Florida during a 12-month period in 1992-93, damaging the $38 billion-a-year industry, the state's most important.
State tourist officials, who spent the weekend fielding media calls from Britain, Germany and other European countries, hit back on Monday.

"We disagree with him strongly on the issue that Florida will be an unsafe place," Miami visitors bureau official Mayco Villafana said. "His logic is faulty in his argument that somehow this is different from what routinely has occured in Florida and other states for years."
After the tourist slayings, statewide tourism dropped 2.8 percent in 1994, but it rebounded by 1995. And in 1996 a record 43 million visitors traveled to the state, up 4.2 percent over 1995.
Florida's government took a series of safety measures including overnight guards at highway rest stops, better road signs and banning special markings on rental cars.
"Tourism officials have worked hard to beef up security for residents and nonresidents," said a spokeswoman for Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles, who criticized McDougall.

"Since 1993, state and local officials have taken a number of aggressive and successful measures to combat crimes against tourists," Bud Nocera, executive vice president of the Florida Tourism Industry Marketing Corp., said. He said crime dropped 11 percent in the past five years.

State officials noted that violent felons leave prison in every state every year, often before the end of their sentences. "To put things in context, and obviously the sheriff did not do this, Florida last year alone released 22,000 inmates," the governor's spokeswoman said.

Last month, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that Florida could not revoke an automatic "gain time" program enacted in the late 1980s to relieve prison overcrowding. The program shortens the time spent in prison by thousands of prisoners, including murderers, rapists and kidnappers.
In the wake of the High Court's ruling, state officials released 300 prisoners last week and were scheduled to free another 200 this week.

In Miami, where some of the most publicized attacks on tourists occurred four years ago, officials said they expected McDougall's remarks would have an impact. "His remarks will have repercussions in the marketplace. He is a professional in law enforcement and therefore his credibility carries weight," Villafana said.
